title: Python Built-in Types & Data Structures: Quick Revision
summary: Revision notes on Python's built-in types, mutability, list/tuple/dict/set operations and their costs, slicing, comprehensions, shallow vs deep copying, and truthiness.

chapters.title: Python Data Model at a Glance
points: Core built-ins: int, float, bool, str, bytes, list, tuple, dict, set, frozenset, NoneType; every value is an object with an identity (id), type and value
Variables are names bound to objects, not boxes holding values: b = a makes two names for one object
Mutable (list, dict, set, bytearray) change in place; immutable (int, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes) never do, so 's += "x"' rebinds to a new object
== compares value, 'is' compares identity; use 'is' only for None, True, False

Hashable = has a __hash__ that never changes and agrees with __eq__ (built-in immutables are hashable, built-in mutable containers are not; user-class instances are hashable by identity by default); only hashable objects can be dict keys or set members (a tuple is hashable only if all its items are)

chapters.title: List and Tuple Operations and Costs
points: list is a dynamic array: index/len/append/pop() are O(1) amortized; insert(0,x), pop(0), remove(x) and 'x in lst' are O(n)
Key methods: append(x), extend(it), insert(i,x), pop(i=-1), remove(x), sort() in place returning None vs sorted() returning a new list
sort/sorted are stable Timsort, O(n log n); key=len or key=lambda t: t[1] picks the sort field, reverse=True flips order
tuple is an immutable fixed-size sequence: used for fixed records, dict keys and multiple return values; unpacking a, *rest = (1,2,3)
Use collections.deque for O(1) pops at both ends; a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,)

chapters.title: Dict and Set Operations and Costs
points: dict and set are hash tables: lookup, insert and delete average O(1), worst case O(n); dict keeps insertion order since 3.7
Safe access: d.get(k, default), d.setdefault(k, []), collections.defaultdict(list), collections.Counter for tallies
Iterate with d.items(), d.keys(), d.values(); merge with d | other or {**a, **b}; never add or remove keys while iterating
Set ops: a | b union, a & b intersection, a - b difference, a ^ b symmetric difference; 'x in set' is O(1) vs O(n) for a list
{} is an empty dict, not a set: use set() for an empty set; set items must be hashable and sets are unordered

chapters.title: Slicing and Comprehensions
points: Slice seq[start:stop:step]: stop is exclusive, negatives count from the end, out-of-range bounds are clamped and never raise
Idioms: s[::-1] reverses, s[:] makes a shallow copy, s[-3:] takes the last three, s[::2] takes every second item; slicing a list copies it in O(k)
Slice assignment lst[1:3] = [9] can resize a list; str and tuple slices return new objects since they are immutable
Comprehensions: [f(x) for x in it if cond], {k: v for ...}, {x for ...}; a condition with else goes before the for: [a if c else b for x in it]
(x for x in it) is a lazy generator using O(1) memory; prefer it inside sum(), any() and all() instead of building a list

chapters.title: Copying and Truthiness
points: b = a copies nothing; both names share one object, so mutating through either is visible through both
Shallow copy (a.copy(), list(a), a[:], copy.copy(a)) makes a new outer container but shares the inner objects
Deep copy copy.deepcopy(a) recursively copies nested objects, so nested edits no longer leak; it is slower and handles cycles
Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, '', [], (), {}, set(), range(0); everything else is truthy, including '0' and [0]
Mutable default argument 'def f(x=[])' is created once and shared across calls: use x=None and create the list inside; [[0]*3]*3 repeats one inner row, so use a comprehension

chapters.title: Built-in Types Cheat Sheet
points: Mutability and hashing: list, dict, set mutable and unhashable; tuple, str, frozenset, int hashable
Costs: list index O(1), list 'in' O(n), dict/set 'in' O(1) average, list insert(0) O(n), sort O(n log n)
Slicing: s[a:b:c], stop exclusive, s[::-1] reverses, s[:] shallow copy
Comprehension forms: [..], {k: v ..}, {..}, (..) generator; copying: assignment shares, copy() is shallow, deepcopy() is full
Truthiness: empty containers, 0, None and '' are falsy; test with 'if items:' and use 'is None' for None checks
